preamble: Diphthongization of a long mid back vowel [oː] into the wide falling diphthong [aʊ̯]: the nucleus lowers and unrounds, and the rounded high offglide stays. In Swabian (Alemannic), Middle High German long ô merged with â and ou into [aʊ̯], giving hoch [hoːx] > hau 'high'. In Mecklenburgish Low German (Schwerin and Western Pomeranian areas), Middle Low German ô is au [ɔʊ]~[aʊ] (tau 'to', bauk 'book'), whereas Strelitz keeps to. The change is rare. Most o-diphthongizations stop at [ou] or [ɔu] (see o_to_ou).

examples.from: Middle High German hôch 'high' (Standard German hoch [hoːx])
examples.note: Middle High German long ô is regularly [aʊ̯] in Swabian, merging with the reflexes of â and ou.

examples.from: Middle High German schône 'already' (Standard German schon [ʃoːn])
examples.note: The same development, with loss of the final nasal.

examples.from: Middle Low German ô, as in Strelitz to 'to' (undiphthongized)
examples.note: The Mecklenburg diphthongization of Middle Low German ô; it is attested in writing since 1734 (tausahmen 'together'). The diphthong is described as [ɔʊ] or [aʊ], a broadening of the general Low German [oʊ] reflex.
Only ô from Proto-Germanic *ō diphthongizes; ô from Proto-Germanic *au stays o (oge 'eye'). Kauken 'cake' shows the same au.
